To: Administrator, CMS | Re: CMS-0062-P | Docket CMS-2026-1255 | From: Joanne Bayouk, MBA, MSN, RN, PMHNP | Just Care | justcare.substack.com I submit these comments as a clinician with over 20 years spanning payer operations, PBM, utilization management, and behavioral health care delivery. Comment 1 &mdash; BH Drugs: The GAO found CMS does not audit BH prior authorization in MA despite 8 of 9 MA organizations requiring it (GAO-25-107342, 2025). Johns Hopkins found PA linked to treatment interruptions, relapse, and worse outcomes in behavioral health (Murphy et al., 2026). CMS must confirm psychiatric and SUD medications are covered, expedited timelines apply for acute BH need, and payers cannot impose more restrictive standards than comparable medical drug classes under MHPAEA. Comment 2 &mdash; FHIR Criteria: Mandating FHIR data exchange while permitting proprietary black-box criteria (InterQual, MCG) defeats the rule&#39;s transparency goal. Clinical decision logic should be expressed in FHIR PlanDefinitions and CQL, derived from APA, SAMHSA, ASAM, and ASCO society guidelines. Transparency in data exchange without transparency in clinical logic is incomplete reform. Comment 3 &mdash; Episode Pilot: 80.7% of appealed PA denials in MA were overturned in 2024 &mdash; the original decision was wrong in the majority of cases (KFF, 2026). I request CMS consider a CMMI demonstration of Episode-Based Behavioral Health Authorization: one PA decision at intake covering the full 90-day episode including evaluation, medication, inpatient stabilization if indicated, PHP, IOP, and follow-up. FHIR-native, society-guideline-anchored, licensed-clinician-governed, compliant with MD HB 1563 and WA SB 5395. Full technical model attached. Comment 4 &mdash; National Scale: This model applies identically to wound care (WOCN/AHRQ) and oncology (ASCO Living Guideline 2026). CMS has the opportunity to establish behavioral health as the proof-of-concept for a national episode authorization standard &mdash; one episode, one authorization, one decision &mdash; across the full spectrum of care. Please refer to attached documents for the full technical model and APA-formatted policy analysis. Joanne Bayouk, MBA, MSN, RN, PMHNP | Just Care | justcare.substack.com | @Just_Care_ | Suwanee, Georgia | June 2026

I strongly support CMS efforts to modernize the prior authorization process and reduce unnecessary administrative barriers to care. Specifically from a workforce and employer perspective,I encourage CMS to ensure that the final rule delivers meaningful operational improvement rather than simply digitizing existing inefficiencies. Nearly 50 million working Americans are simultaneously serving as family caregivers while managing full-time employment responsibilities. Delays, denials, repetitive documentation requests, and unclear authorization processes often require caregivers to spend hours coordinating care, contacting insurers, navigating appeals, and managing treatment disruptions. These burdens affect not only patients and families, but also workforce productivity, employee wellbeing, absenteeism, retention, and healthcare-related financial stress. For this reason, I strongly encourage CMS to preserve meaningful response timelines and avoid weakening key implementation requirements during the final rulemaking process. Timely decision-making is essential to reducing disruption for working caregivers and maintaining continuity of care. I also encourage CMS to maintain strong transparency requirements regarding denial rates, approval timelines, and appeal outcomes. Without measurable accountability, interoperability improvements may improve administrative systems without materially improving patient or caregiver experience. In addition, CMS should discourage repetitive prior authorization requirements for chronic, stable, or previously approved therapies. Repeated reauthorization requirements frequently consume substantial time for caregivers, providers, and patients without improving care quality. As automated and AI-assisted authorization systems become more common, CMS should also ensure that technology is used to streamline care access rather than accelerate denials or reduce individualized clinical review. This proposal presents an important opportunity to improve not only healthcare administration, but also workforce stability and caregiver support across the United States.

As a three-time cancer survivor living with Lynch Syndrome (MSH2 mutation), I understand firsthand the importance of timely access to laboratory testing. Throughout my cancer journey, laboratory, pathology, biomarker, and genetic testing have guided critical healthcare decisions that impacted my treatment, surveillance, and long-term health outcomes. Prior authorization requirements can create unnecessary delays in obtaining medically necessary tests. For patients facing a cancer diagnosis or potential disease progression, every day spent waiting for approval can increase anxiety, delay treatment decisions, and postpone access to potentially life-saving interventions. Biomarker and genomic testing are particularly important in modern cancer care because they help identify targeted therapies, determine eligibility for clinical trials, and support personalized treatment decisions. These tests are often ordered based on established clinical guidelines and evidence-based standards of care. Requiring additional administrative approval for guideline-recommended testing can create barriers that ultimately undermine the promise of precision medicine. Prior authorization requirements may also disproportionately affect patients in underserved communities, those with limited health literacy, older adults, and individuals who already face challenges navigating a complex healthcare system. Patients should not have to become insurance experts in order to access medically necessary testing recommended by their healthcare providers. In addition to delays, prior authorization can contribute to duplicated testing, repeated blood draws, additional appointments, and increased administrative burden on clinicians and healthcare staff. These inefficiencies increase costs while adding stress to patients and families already coping with serious illness. CMS should consider policies that exempt guideline-supported laboratory testing, biomarker testing, and genetic testing from prior authorization requirements when ordered according to nationally recognized clinical guidelines. CMS should also promote greater transparency, faster decision-making timelines, and standardized approval processes to ensure that patients receive timely access to medically necessary care. As both a Patient and Advocate, I believe healthcare decisions should be driven by clinical evidence and patient need rather than administrative barriers. Timely access to laboratory testing can improve outcomes, reduce disparities, and help ensure that patients receive the right care at the right time. Had genetic testing been available and utilized more broadly earlier in my family&#39;s history, my Lynch Syndrome diagnosis may have been identified sooner, potentially influencing screening decisions and risk management for myself and other family members. Timely access to testing does not just affect one patient&mdash;it can affect entire families across generations. When access to laboratory testing is delayed, diagnosis is delayed. When diagnosis is delayed, treatment is delayed. And when treatment is delayed, patients bear the consequences.

To Whom It May Concern: I respectfully submit the following comments regarding CMS-0062-P. I support CMS&#39;s efforts to improve prior authorization processes and reduce barriers to healthcare access. As a social work professional serving individuals with disabilities and chronic health conditions, I have observed firsthand the challenges that prior authorization requirements can create for vulnerable populations. I am specifically commenting on the section addressing prior authorization requirements for Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics, and Supplies (DMEPOS). CMS appropriately recognizes that prior authorization processes may delay access to medically necessary equipment and seeks public feedback on ways to reduce these burdens. Individuals with disabilities often depend on wheelchairs, prosthetic devices, orthotic equipment, and other assistive technologies to maintain independence, employment, community participation, and health. Delays in obtaining these items can have significant consequences. When prior authorization decisions are delayed, beneficiaries may experience decreased mobility, increased risk of injury, deterioration of health conditions, and reduced quality of life. I recommend that CMS establish an expedited review process for replacement or modification of previously approved durable medical equipment when medical necessity has already been documented and remains substantially unchanged. Many beneficiaries must repeatedly demonstrate medical necessity for equipment that has long been recognized as essential to daily functioning. This requirement creates administrative burdens for beneficiaries, providers, and payers while offering limited additional value in preventing inappropriate utilization. Additionally, I recommend that CMS consider multi-year authorization periods for certain categories of durable medical equipment used by individuals with permanent disabilities. Conditions such as spinal cord injuries, limb loss, and congenital disabilities often involve lifelong needs that do not require repeated reassessment. Extended authorization periods could reduce administrative costs while maintaining appropriate program oversight. I also support CMS&#39;s efforts to increase transparency regarding prior authorization decisions and denial explanations. Clear communication regarding the reasons for denial can assist beneficiaries and providers in understanding documentation requirements and pursuing timely appeals when necessary. Transparent decision-making promotes accountability and may reduce unnecessary delays in care. Finally, I encourage CMS to continue engaging disability advocates, healthcare providers, and social workers during implementation of any final rule. These stakeholders possess valuable practical knowledge regarding the real-world effects of prior authorization requirements and can help identify opportunities for improvement. Thank you for considering these comments. I appreciate CMS&#39;s commitment to improving healthcare access and reducing unnecessary administrative burdens for beneficiaries. I respectfully request that CMS incorporate additional protections for individuals requiring durable medical equipment and other long-term supports as it develops the final rule. Sincerely, Heidi Wachtel MSW Student

Hello, I am submitting this comment as an undergraduate student pursuing dual degrees in Public Health and Mathematical Data Science at San Diego State University, where I am also involved in public health research focused on infectious disease modeling, community health impact assessment, and health equity in underserved border communities. I strongly support the proposed rule&#39;s expansion of interoperability standards and electronic prior authorization (ePA) requirements to Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid managed care plans, and CHIP agencies. This rule addresses a critical bottleneck in the healthcare system, one that disproportionately harms the most vulnerable patients. Prior authorization delays are not &quot;administrative inconveniences&quot;. Research has consistently shown that PA burdens fall hardest on Medicaid beneficiaries, who are more likely to be patients of color, low-income, and reliant on community health centers with limited administrative capacity to manage PA workflows. In border communities like those along the San Diego&ndash;Tijuana corridor, where I have conducted community health research, these barriers compound existing access inequities. A patient waiting days or weeks for PA approval on a necessary medication may forgo care entirely with downstream consequences for chronic disease management, emergency utilization, and population health outcomes. The proposed FHIR-based standards for drug PA are a meaningful step toward reducing this burden. Standardized electronic PA workflows would reduce the time providers spend on administrative tasks, accelerate decisions for patients, and generate structured data that public health researchers and policymakers can use to monitor disparities in PA approval rates across demographic groups and plan types. However, I urge CMS to go further in two areas: First, the proposed rule should require plans to publicly report PA approval and denial rates, stratified by race, ethnicity, language, and condition type. Without this data transparency, it is impossible to identify and correct discriminatory patterns in PA decision-making. The rule&#39;s interoperability infrastructure makes this reporting technically feasible &mdash; CMS should require it. Second, I urge CMS to set meaningful timelines for drug PA decisions that reflect clinical urgency. The proposed rule is an opportunity to establish enforceable standards that protect patients when delays can cause measurable harm. I commend CMS for advancing this rulemaking and urge the agency to finalize it with strong equity provisions. Health data infrastructure is only as valuable as the health outcomes it produces, and this rule has the potential to meaningfully reduce disparities if implemented with that goal in mind. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Dear CMS, I am a technology leader and IEEE Senior Member with experience supporting AI adoption across 180 or more organizations in healthcare, enterprise, and public sector environments. My peer reviewed research on secure AI architectures for healthcare critical infrastructure was published at IEEE SoutheastCon 2026, and I have written for Healthcare IT Today on post deployment AI governance. I am submitting this comment based on practical experience with AI driven automation in regulated healthcare environments. My comments focus on sections II.B (Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs) and II.C (Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations). 1. Prior authorization decisions that involve AI need transparency at the decision layer Prior authorization for drugs is increasingly automated on the payer side. AI is used to triage, recommend, or deny requests before a human ever looks at the file. When AI contributes to a denial or an adverse determination, the specific reason for denial requirements in this rule should extend to the AI layer itself. That means disclosing the model version in use at the time of the decision, the inputs it considered, and whether a human actually reviewed the determination before it was sent out. The proposed public reporting of denial and appeal metrics is a strong step. Without transparency at the decision layer, though, those metrics will describe the outcome but not how the outcome was produced. Patients, prescribers, and pharmacists receive the answer without the decision process behind it, which limits what any of them can do with the information. 2. FHIR based Prior Authorization API requirements should be paired with AI metadata The FHIR first direction of this rule, including the proposed adoption of the CRD, DTR, and PAS implementation guides for the Prior Authorization API, is strong. As payers and providers exchange data to support electronic prior authorization for drugs covered under a medical benefit, the data envelope should carry enough metadata to identify when AI was used in a decision path. Existing FHIR resources can be extended to carry this metadata without a redesign of the implementation guides CMS is proposing to require. This is consistent with where HTI-5 was heading on automated actor recognition and with broader federal AI governance work under the NIST AI RMF. Carrying AI metadata in the same transactions that already carry prior authorization decisions avoids standing up a parallel disclosure channel later. 3. Vendor accountability applies to AI enabled prior authorization Many impacted payers deploy AI for prior authorization through third party vendors, including pharmacy benefit managers and utilization management vendors. The contracts with those vendors were usually written for traditional rules engines, not adaptive AI. Model updates, training data provenance, and ongoing performance monitoring typically are not covered. As CMS establishes the October 1, 2027 compliance dates, the electronic prior authorization requirements, and the decision timeframes in this rule, it is worth addressing vendor accountability for the AI components of the decision pipeline. Otherwise the impacted payer carries the regulatory burden for behavior it does not fully control, and the provider has no clear entity to engage with when something goes wrong. 4. Continuous monitoring of denial and appeal patterns The proposed public reporting requirements for prior authorization for drugs would be stronger with a continuous monitoring expectation built in. Impacted payers could track and report on denial rates, appeal reversal rates, and decision timing by drug category and patient population. That kind of monitoring creates an operational feedback loop that helps surface when AI driven systems are producing unintended patterns, rather than waiting for those patterns to show up in complaints, state enforcement, or litigation. It also aligns with the direction the proposed numeric count metrics are already moving in. Thank you for the opportunity to contribute. Sincerely, Pooja Walia IEEE Senior Member Author, ICLR/ICML Reviewer Published research: &quot;Building Secure and Trustworthy AI for Healthcare Critical Infrastructure,&quot; IEEE SoutheastCon 2026

As a healthcare leader responsible for clinical informatics and operational workflows, I strongly support the intent of this proposed rule to modernize prior authorization through improved interoperability and electronic processes. Prior authorization delays are not simply administrative inefficiencies&mdash;they directly impact patient care. When approvals are delayed, patients experience postponed treatments, interruptions in medication access, and, in some cases, worsening clinical outcomes. For this reason, the proposed decision timeframes are not just operational benchmarks; they are critical patient safety safeguards. However, the effectiveness of this rule will depend on meaningful enforcement. If payers are not held accountable to consistently meet these timelines, the burden of delay will continue to fall on patients despite the transition to electronic systems. Additionally, it is essential that payers bear the primary responsibility for the costs and operational lift associated with integration and implementation. Prior authorization requirements originate from payer policies, and the administrative complexity that this rule seeks to address has largely been driven by payer processes. While providers will need to interact with enhanced digital workflows, shifting the cost burden onto health systems would further strain organizations already managing significant clinical and financial pressures. True reform requires clear accountability&mdash;both in terms of adherence to required timelines and investment in the infrastructure needed to support interoperability. Without enforceable standards and appropriate allocation of responsibility, there is a risk that these changes will not achieve their intended impact. Ensuring payer accountability will be key to delivering meaningful improvements in efficiency, transparency, and, most importantly, patient care.

Date: June 8, 2026 To: Centers for Medicare &amp; Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services Attention: Docket ID: CMS-2026-1255 Reference: RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to Laboratory Testing (Section III.E of CMS-0062-P) Submission Portal: Regulations.gov Re: Comment on RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to Laboratory Testing Sample Letter (please customize to make this uniquely your own) To Whom It May Concern: My name is Ashleigh Parker and I am writing as a cancer patient in remission to urgently request that CMS protect patients from critical care delays and denials caused by rigid prior authorization requirements for laboratory testing. As a cancer patient since 2019, I understand the speed at which care should be provided to cancer patients. The quicker cancer is found and treated, the better the outcome is for the patient. Biomarker testing improves these outcomes. I am a living example of that. We commend CMS for its ongoing efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization processes. We also deeply appreciate the opportunity to provide specific feedback via the Request for Information regarding the impact of prior authorization on timely patient access to medically necessary laboratory testing, as referenced in Section III.E of CMS-0062-P. I urge CMS to protect oncology patients from delays and denials caused by prior authorization requirements for medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing. In cancer care, timing is critical. Biomarker and specialty lab results often guide treatment selection, treatment changes, disease monitoring, and clinical trial eligibility. When prior authorization rules require approval before or on the exact specimen collection date, valid specimens may be delayed, rejected, or discarded&mdash;even when the patient, physician, and laboratory acted in good faith. This can force repeat blood draws and delay urgent cancer care. CMS should require health plans to: 1. Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected. 2. Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing. 3. Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available. 4. Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing. 5. Protect patients from surprise costs when delays are administrative. Cancer patients need timely access to laboratory testing so they and their care teams can make informed, potentially life-saving treatment decisions without unnecessary administrative barriers. Sincerely, Ashleigh Parker Stage 4 Colorectal Cancer Survivor Olive Branch,MS

CMS should advance interoperable electronic exchange of clinical information as part of prior authorization workflows to reduce administrative burden, improve interoperability, and accelerate patient access to therapy. Two complementary approaches could support CMS goals for more efficient and near real-time prior authorization adjudication across pharmacy and medical benefit workflows: 1. Prospective clinical data exchange at the time of prior authorization submission: As part of the initial prior authorization request from the prescriber, CMS should require the transmission of relevant patient clinical data through interoperable standards, including NCPDP SCRIPT ePA for pharmacy benefit drugs and HL7 FHIR-based prior authorization workflows for medical services and drugs covered under the medical benefit. For pharmacy workflows, Real-Time Benefit Tool (RTBT) capabilities leveraging the NCPDP RTPB standard are necessary to identify the applicable pharmacy benefit, determine whether prior authorization is required, and support routing through the appropriate electronic prior authorization workflow. For medical services and medical-benefit drugs, HL7 FHIR-based workflows can support identification of coverage requirements and facilitate exchange of the clinical information necessary to support prior authorization review. Enabling prospective exchange of structured clinical data at the point of submission would support faster and more accurate prior authorization determinations, reduce manual documentation requests, minimize administrative burden on providers and payers, and promote faster access to therapy and improved patient outcomes. 2. TEFCA-enabled clinical data exchange for prior authorization workflows: To support both prospective and retrospective prior authorization workflows, CMS and ONC should clarify that prior authorization constitutes an appropriate TEFCA Purpose of Use that permits and requires the exchange of patient clinical data necessary to support prior authorization review and adjudication. Without clear TEFCA policy alignment requiring exchange of clinical information for prior authorization workflows, EHR systems and healthcare organizations may continue to restrict or block sharing of the patient clinical data necessary to support interoperable prior authorization processes. Clarifying TEFCA requirements for prior authorization-related data exchange would enable more consistent sharing of clinical information across pharmacy and medical workflows, reduce provider and payer burden, and advance CMS goals for streamlined and near real-time prior authorization adjudication.

May 22, 2026 Centers for Medicare &amp; Medicaid Services Re: CMS-0062-P &mdash; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Docket No. CMS-2026-1255 Dear Office of CMS, I am a retail pharmacist, and I am submitting this comment in support of the proposed rule CMS-0062-P. I work directly with patients, doctors, and insurance companies every day, and I want to share what I see on the ground when it comes to prior authorization for prescription drugs. The current prior authorization process is slow and burdensome for everyone involved. When a doctor sends a prescription and the drug requires prior authorization, the pharmacy has to call the doctor&#39;s office to notify them and then keep calling back to find out whether they have submitted the authorization and whether it has been approved. The pharmacy does not always have visibility into what stage the process is at or whether the doctor has even contacted the insurance company. This follow-up takes up a significant amount of pharmacy staff time that should be spent on patient care. At the same time, CMS estimates that prior authorization costs providers around $34,000 and 700 hours per year in administrative work. While all of this is happening, the patient is sitting and waiting for their medicine with no idea what is going on or how long it will take. I strongly support moving prior authorization for drugs to a fully electronic process. However, I would like to suggest three specific improvements to make this proposal more effective. First, patients need to be included in the notification process. Right now, when a prior authorization request is sent to a doctor through systems like CoverMyMeds, the patient receives no notification at all. The proposal should require that when a prior authorization is initiated, the patient automatically receives a notification so they know what is happening and can follow up if needed. Transparency for the patient is just as important as speed. Second, providers should be given real-time access to each patient&#39;s drug formulary before writing a prescription. If a doctor could check what the patient&#39;s insurance covers and initiate prior authorization before sending the prescription to the pharmacy, the entire back-and-forth process between the pharmacy and the doctor&#39;s office could be avoided. This would save time for both the pharmacy and the provider, and most importantly, it would reduce the wait time for the patient. Third, I have a concern about the API reporting requirement and the civil monetary penalties attached to it. While I understand the need for accountability, adding penalty-backed reporting requirements creates a new administrative burden for providers. When providers are focused on managing compliance and avoiding penalties, their attention shifts away from patient care, which is the opposite of what this proposal is trying to achieve. I would ask CMS to consider whether there is a simpler way to monitor compliance that does not add to the administrative load that providers are already carrying. Overall, I believe this proposal is a step in the right direction. The prior authorization process for drugs needs to be modernized, and I am glad CMS is addressing it. I hope these suggestions are helpful, and I appreciate the opportunity to comment. Respectfully

I am nurse practitioner in Florida. Prior authorization (PA) and step therapy requirements create significant barriers to timely patient care. While utilization management can play a role in promoting evidence-based care, the current processes frequently result in treatment delays, interruptions in therapy, increased administrative burden, and patient frustration. Prior authorization requirements often delay medically necessary treatment while patients wait for payer review and approval. Step therapy policies can require patients to fail therapies that may be less effective or inappropriate for their individual clinical circumstances before accessing the treatment recommended by their clinician. These challenges are particularly burdensome for physician-administered therapies, where delays can postpone treatment initiation and worsen patient outcomes. In addition, health plans may implement coverage policy changes with limited advance notice, creating confusion for patients and providers and disrupting continuity of care. Specific Patient Example One of my patients required a physician-administered therapy that I determined was medically appropriate based on clinical guidelines and the patient&#39;s treatment history. However, the patient&#39;s health plan required prior authorization and additional documentation. The approval process took several weeks, during which the patient&#39;s symptoms worsened and additional office visits were required. Significant staff time was also spent responding to payer requests and appeals. Ultimately, the therapy was approved, but the delay created unnecessary burden for both the patient and the care team. Provisions of the Proposed Rule I Support I strongly support several aspects of CMS&#39;s proposed rule. Faster prior authorization decisions: More timely determinations would help reduce treatment delays and improve patient access to medically necessary care. CMS has proposed measures intended to accelerate payer decision-making and improve the prior authorization process. Expanded electronic prior authorization (e-PA): Requiring standardized electronic prior authorization processes and APIs has the potential to reduce administrative burden, improve workflow efficiency, and facilitate real-time information exchange between providers and health plans. Greater health plan transparency: Public reporting of prior authorization metrics and clearer communication regarding denials will help providers and patients better understand coverage requirements and hold plans accountable for timely and appropriate decision-making. Recommendations for CMS to Strengthen the Rule I encourage CMS to further strengthen the rule by: Requiring advance notice of coverage policy and formulary changes that affect physician-administered therapies. Limiting step therapy requirements when evidence supports the prescribed therapy or when patients have already demonstrated failure, intolerance, or contraindications to alternative treatments. Ensuring that prior authorization and step therapy decisions are based on current clinical evidence and specialty-specific guidelines. Expanding protections that preserve continuity of care when patients change health plans. Requiring greater transparency around approval, denial, and overturn rates for both prior authorization and step therapy requests. Establishing stronger oversight and accountability mechanisms when plans fail to meet required response timeframes. Closing As a nurse practitioner, I support CMS&#39;s efforts to modernize prior authorization through faster decisions, expanded electronic prior authorization capabilities, and increased transparency. These reforms can help reduce administrative burden and improve patient access to timely, evidence-based care. However, additional protections are needed to ensure that prior authorization and step therapy policies do not interfere with clinically appropriate treatment decisions made by healthcare providers in partnership with their patients. Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments.

Date: June 8, 2026 To: Centers for Medicare &amp; Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services Attention: Docket ID: CMS-2026-1255 Reference: RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to Laboratory Testing (Section III.E of CMS-0062-P) Submission Portal: Regulations.gov Re: Comment on RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to Laboratory Testing Sample Letter (please customize to make this uniquely your own) To Whom It May Concern: My name is Ashleigh Parker and I am writing as a cancer patient in remission to urgently request that CMS protect patients from critical care delays and denials caused by rigid prior authorization requirements for laboratory testing. As a cancer patient since 2019, I understand the speed at which care should be provided to cancer patients. The quicker cancer is found and treated, the better the outcome is for the patient. Biomarker testing improves these outcomes. I am a living example of that. We commend CMS for its ongoing efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization processes. We also deeply appreciate the opportunity to provide specific feedback via the Request for Information regarding the impact of prior authorization on timely patient access to medically necessary laboratory testing, as referenced in Section III.E of CMS-0062-P. I urge CMS to protect oncology patients from delays and denials caused by prior authorization requirements for medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing. In cancer care, timing is critical. Biomarker and specialty lab results often guide treatment selection, treatment changes, disease monitoring, and clinical trial eligibility. When prior authorization rules require approval before or on the exact specimen collection date, valid specimens may be delayed, rejected, or discarded&mdash;even when the patient, physician, and laboratory acted in good faith. This can force repeat blood draws and delay urgent cancer care. CMS should require health plans to: 1. Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected. 2. Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing. 3. Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available. 4. Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing. 5. Protect patients from surprise costs when delays are administrative. Cancer patients need timely access to laboratory testing so they and their care teams can make informed, potentially life-saving treatment decisions without unnecessary administrative barriers. Sincerely, Ashleigh Parker Stage 4 Colorectal Cancer Survivor Olive Branch,MS

To better align insurance policies with real-world clinical workflows, we request that CMS mandate that health plans: &bull; Allow Retroactive Approvals. Ensure that necessary lab tests conducted during urgent care visits are eligible for coverage without risk of arbitrary retroactive denial. &bull; Prohibit Timing-Based Denials. Prevent insurers from rejecting claims solely due to strict calendar or timing constraints, which often conflict with individualized diabetes care. &bull; Eliminate Redundant Testing. Require coordinated care networks to accept recent, comprehensive laboratory results to avoid unnecessary, repetitive blood draws. &bull; Establish Expedited Pathways. Create swift, streamlined approval processes for medically necessary, time-sensitive continuous glucose monitoring and laboratory data. &bull; Protect Patients Financially. Cap out-of-pocket costs and protect patients from unexpected billing when prior authorization delays or administrative errors occur Individuals managing diabetes require timely, continuous access to laboratory data. Prior authorization frameworks must promote patient health rather than function as administrative barriers. Thank you for your consideration of these critical recommendations. Sincerely, Mutima Jackson-Anderson, Executive Director Ruby A. Neeson Diabetes Awareness Foundation

Re: CMS-0062-P, 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs (91 FR 19890) EVRESA LLC (Enterprise Verification - Regulated E-Settlement Architecture) submits the attached public comment package on CMS-0062-P, RIN 0938-AV44: a foundational comment, three RFI responses, and an Operational Impact Statement on independent community pharmacy. EVRESA is an AI-governance infrastructure developer building CATN, the Care Access Trust Network by EVRESA, a governance and decision-provenance layer for prior authorization. EVRESA submits this comment as a developer of governance infrastructure, not as a payer or provider; our perspective is architectural. EVRESA strongly supports extending electronic prior authorization to drugs, aligning decision timeframes, and requiring a specific reason for each denial. EVRESA writes to identify one implementation gap that will determine whether these gains are durable: the proposed rule standardizes the transaction of a prior authorization decision, but not the governance proof layer needed to establish accountability for that decision where automated or AI-enabled tools are used. To meet 72-hour and 24-hour timeframes, impacted payers and technology partners may increasingly place automated, rules-based, or AI-enabled systems in the decision loop. A specific denial reason is necessary, but it is not sufficient by itself. A denial reason does not establish who or what rendered the decision, whether AI contributed, what evidence was reviewed, under whose authority the decision was made, or whether a qualified human remained accountable at the decision point. Without governance-layer controls, a denial reason can become a machine-generated field attached to an unaccountable automated decision. EVRESA recommends that CMS recognize, in the final rule preamble or subsequent implementation guidance, privacy-preserving governance-layer controls above the transaction layer standardized by CMS-0062-P. These controls should include decision provenance, human-authority attestation, tamper-evident audit records, evidence-chain integrity, and a verifiable chain of custody for decision evidence. First, CMS should encourage decision provenance records for drug prior authorization determinations where automated or AI-enabled tools are used, including a structured, machine-verifiable record of which system rendered or supported the decision, whether AI contributed, what evidence was reviewed, and which human authority was accountable for the outcome. Second, CMS should encourage denial reasons to be bound to provenance records where feasible, so appeals, audits, and oversight can verify that a denial was not an unreviewed automated action. Third, in response to RFI III.B on Increasing Health Care Resiliency, CMS should treat the integrity and auditability of the prior authorization decision record as a resiliency control. Resiliency is not only uptime; it is the ability to prove, after the fact, that decisions affecting patient access were made under valid authority through a verifiable chain of custody for decision evidence. Fourth, CMS should encourage testable governance outcomes. Provenance, human-authority, evidence-chain, and tamper-evident audit controls should be verifiable through implementation testing, not self-attestation alone. These recommendations do not require CMS to mandate EVRESA, CATN, or any specific vendor, platform, ledger, or architecture. They define a vendor-neutral outcome: where automated or AI-enabled tools are used, every prior authorization decision should be attributable, authority-bound, evidence-linked, privacy-preserving, and auditable. EVRESA&#39;s design pattern operationalizes this principle as Human Authority, Enforced at Machine Speed, and is offered as one reference model among many possible implementations. As CMS modernizes prior authorization to protect patient access, the same automation that creates speed also creates a new governance risk: speed without accountability. Governance-layer controls allow CMS and the healthcare ecosystem to capture the benefits of automation while preserving the human authority, evidence integrity, privacy, and auditability that make prior authorization decisions trustworthy. Respectfully submitted, John Gray Rodriguez Founder &amp; Chief Executive Officer EVRESA LLC Care Access Trust Network (CATN) by EVRESA File Code: CMS-0062-P Docket No. CMS-2026-1255

I am writing to submit comments on the proposed rule CMS-0062-P. I am a rheumatologist in Seattle, Washington, and I conduct research on prior authorization barriers in rheumatology, including published studies on tocilizumab access delays in giant cell arteritis and carrier-level variation in PA approval rates for biologic medications. I submit these comments as an individual physician and researcher. I strongly support the goals of this proposed rule. I. Clinical Urgency: Drug PA in Rheumatology Cannot Wait 7 Days PA delays for biologic medications cause measurable patient harm. Visual loss in Giant Cell Arteritis can occur within hours. A 7-calendar-day standard decision window for non-urgent drug PA may be insufficient for this and similar conditions requiring urgent biologics. (Bays et al., J Rheumatol 2025, PMID 40089304.) Recommendation: &bull; Create an explicit expedited drug PA pathway for conditions with acute risk of organ damage or death, with a 24-48 hour decision standard. &bull; Define expedited eligibility criteria that include vision-threatening disease, acute inflammatory flares with functional impairment, and other conditions where delay risks irreversible harm. II. Electronic Transmission Is Not Enough &mdash; Denial Content Must Be Meaningful Electronic submission of inadequate denial rationales does not advance transparency. In research analyzing Washington State&#39;s mandatory PA transparency dataset &mdash; the only publicly available drug-level PA dataset in the United States &mdash; I found approval rates for the same biologic drug ranging from 2.3% to 100% across carriers, a 44-fold variation that cannot be explained by clinical appropriateness alone. Opaque, inconsistent decision-making is not cured by digitizing it. Recommendation: Require that drug PA denial notices include: &bull; The specific formulary criterion or clinical policy provision that was not met, cited by name and version. &bull; Whether the denial is based on step therapy, and which specific prior drug trials are required. &bull; Whether an AI or algorithmic tool was used in the decision, and if so, which system. &bull; The name and specialty of the reviewing clinician for peer-to-peer denials. Generic &#39;not medically necessary&#39; denials communicated electronically are no improvement over paper denials. The rule should specify minimum content standards for denial explanations. III. Step Therapy for Biologics Requires Specific Standards Step therapy &mdash; requiring patients to fail on a lower-cost drug before a prescribed biologic is authorized &mdash; is one of the most disruptive PA practices in rheumatology. It delays guideline-concordant care and in some cases results in preventable joint damage or organ injury during the mandated &#39;fail first&#39; period. Recommendation: &bull; Require payers to publish step therapy protocols for each drug at each formulary tier in a standardized, machine-readable format. &bull; Establish gold card exemptions for patients with documented completion of required step therapy in prior claims data, eliminating redundant re-authorization for the same drug class. &bull; Prohibit prospective re-trials of drugs a patient has already documented failure on. IV. Drug-Level PA Data Should Be Publicly Reported Washington State&#39;s mandatory PA transparency law is the only mechanism in the United States producing drug-specific, carrier-level PA approval and denial data. The variation it reveals &mdash; which is not visible in aggregate statistics &mdash; is essential for accountability and health services research. CMS is positioned to create a centralized, publicly accessible drug PA data repository that does not currently exist at the federal level. Recommendation: Require public reporting of drug PA metrics at the drug-specific and carrier-specific level, and establish a centralized CMS repository for this data &mdash; modeled on the transparency provisions of state laws like Washington&#39;s ESSB 6404. CMS-0062-P is an important step toward holding payers accountable for drug PA practices that cause measurable patient harm. Strengthening the rule with expedited pathways for urgent biologics, meaningful denial content standards, step therapy transparency, an accelerated Medicare Advantage timeline, and drug-level public reporting would substantially improve outcomes for patients with autoimmune and rheumatic diseases. I am grateful for the opportunity to comment and am available to provide additional information. Respectfully submitted, Dr. Bays

Prior approval delays treatment. Worse, denial of treatment prevents us from getting the treatment we need. The Medicare coverage of life-saving drugs is also an issue. For example, Eliquis is a needed blood thinner for many cancer patients. It is either not covered or poorly covered, costing patients hundreds of dollars a month that many on social security do not have to spare. Less effective and more dangerous drugs (Warfarin) are covered but have worse side effects and require blood testing every 4-6 weeks.

2026-06-10 · ID: CMS-2026-1255-0055
As a Maternal-Fetal Medicine physician, I strongly support CMS&rsquo;s efforts to reform prior authorization requirements for diagnostic laboratory testing. In high-risk obstetrics, timely access to prenatal genetic screening and diagnostic testing is critical. Current prior authorization practices often delay medically necessary testing, force repeat blood draws, and create unnecessary stress for pregnant patients. Denying coverage because authorization was pending on the day a specimen was collected serves no clinical purpose and can delay important medical decisions. I encourage CMS to: &bull; Prohibit timing-based denials when testing is medically necessary. &bull; Eliminate unnecessary repeat blood draws caused by administrative delays. &bull; Require expedited review pathways for prenatal, oncology, and other time-sensitive diagnostic testing. &bull; Protect patients and providers from financial penalties resulting from insurance processing delays. These reforms would improve patient care, reduce administrative burden, and help ensure that patients receive timely access to medically necessary testing. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, Nima Goharkhay, MD, PHD Maternal-Fetal Medicine

From the payer perspective, prior authorization is an important policy tool to help ensure services are medically necessary, clinically appropriate, and consistent with coverage requirements, while also helping prevent fraud, waste, and abuse. This includes targeted oversight of high-risk durable medical equipment and laboratory services where billing patterns may indicate overutilization, duplicative testing, excessive repeat orders, provision without sufficient documentation of medical necessity, or other potentially fraudulent or wasteful practices. At the same time, consistent with the goals reflected in the Centers for Medicare &amp; Medicaid Services proposed rule CMS-0062-P, the prior authorization process should be as streamlined, timely, transparent, and electronically enabled as possible in order to reduce provider burden and avoid unnecessary delays in care. Prior authorization programs should support clear clinical criteria, prompt determinations for urgent and standard requests, transparent communication of approval and denial rationale, and standardized electronic workflows that improve efficiency while preserving program integrity safeguards.
